The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p99 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:24:11Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:24:34Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:18:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-11T03:25:24Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 7 minutes 24 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 3 minutes 33 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:28:05Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.2% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.2% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.0% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none - no more of the traffic failed while it was broken than before it began.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p99 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 198.36666666666667 ms {series_before} before it began, 1406 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 2083 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T03:24:32Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T03:24:50Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T03:24:51Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T03:24:57Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 03:24:11 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T03:25:01Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T03:25:02Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:18 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T03:25:02Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T03:25:04Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 03:19 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T03:25:05Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 1 {T9.2} production change
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T03:25:05Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read the service register - the service calls io-pricing (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-summary-cache (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-pay (third-party, owned by IO Payments Ltd)
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T03:25:06Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 36 {T11.2} minutes 11 {T11.3} seconds before 03:24:11 {T11.4}
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T03:25:06Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 134 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T03:25:08Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T13.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T03:25:08Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T03:25:08Z {T15.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T15.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T15.3} hour before 03:25:08 {T15.4}
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T03:25:12Z {T16.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T03:25:13Z {T17.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T03:25:24Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1, moved from ON to OFF
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T03:25:31Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 03:26 {T19.2} - up to 215s {T19.3}
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T03:28:05Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:25 {T20.2}
  - [T21] 2026-11-11T03:28:05Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T22] 2026-11-11T03:28:05Z {T22.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - set flag [typical-purchase-feature] OFF and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T23] 2026-11-11T03:29:52Z {T23.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/545

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-11T03:18:23Z {P1.1} flag-toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [Ga6f5] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 {Ga6f5.1} evaluations - 30 {Ga6f5.2} occurrences in 30 {Ga6f5.3} minutes, 02:48–03:17 {Ga6f5.4}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 60 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 37 {G46bc.2} minutes, 02:48–03:24 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 34 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 37 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 02:48–03:24 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 2.50% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.00% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 02:59 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 3 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 31 {Gad41.2} minutes, 02:49–03:19 {Gad41.3}
  - [Gc8c4] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 77 {Gc8c4.1} / on 123 {Gc8c4.2} - 200 {Gc8c4.3} evaluations - 1 {Gc8c4.4} occurrence in 1 {Gc8c4.5} minute, 03:18 {Gc8c4.6}
  - [Gd44a] INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 {Gd44a.1} evaluations - 6 {Gd44a.2} occurrences in 6 {Gd44a.3} minutes, 03:19–03:24 {Gd44a.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] The feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched from off to on at 2026-11-11T03:18:23Z {C1.1}. From that minute p99 latency rose from about 200ms {C1.2} to between 750ms {C1.3} and 2083ms {C1.4}. Error rate, p50, p95, memory, CPU and traffic stayed at baseline. No deployment or placement change accompanied it. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.88 {C1.5}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py. `typical_spend_per_item` is the function `render_spend_summary` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py calls when `use_typical_spend` is true. To find the middle price it ran `remaining.remove(min(remaining))` (n-1)//2 times. Each pass scans the whole list for the minimum and then scans it again to remove that element, so the work grows with the square of the history's length. For shoppers with a short history that cost is small. For shoppers with a long history it is large. That fits a p99-only rise from the moment the flag sent requests into this path, with p50 and p95 flat. The flag only exposed it: any request routed here would have paid this cost.
      
      The change: sort the prices once and take index (len - 1 {F1.1}) // 2 {F1.2}. That is O(n log n) and gives the same answer the loop did: the lower of the two middles on an even-length history, with each repeated price counted once per purchase. For an empty history the old code raised ValueError from `min([])`. The new code raises ValueError itself, so callers that handle that see the same exception type as before. The function's signature and the caller in spend_summary.py are unchanged.
      
      The test: tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py keeps its existing correctness cases and adds two. The first is a bound on work. It builds a shuffled 2000-purchase history from an int subclass that counts `<` and `==` comparisons, and asserts the count stays under 4·n·log2(n). The remove-the-minimum loop needs roughly n²/2 comparisons (about two million here) and is written to exceed the bound. A single sort is written to fit well inside it. The second checks that an empty history still raises ValueError.
      
      Not changed: `average_spend_per_item` in spend_summary.py also re-sums a prefix on every pass, which is quadratic too. That is the long-standing flag-off path, not the one this flag switched on, so I left it alone to keep this diff small. It deserves its own follow-up.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #545 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: With use_typical_spend true, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). Code-Fix read that function as finding the middle price by repeatedly scanning the whole purchase history for its minimum and then scanning it again to remove it, many times over. Its work therefore grows far faster than the history's length, so requests for shoppers with long histories pay a large cost. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a feature made the shop use a new way of working out a shopper's typical spend, and that method likely slows down sharply for shoppers with a long purchase history, so their pages took much longer to load.
still_at_risk: Switching typical-purchase-feature back on, or sending any other request to the typical-spend calculation, could again make requests for shoppers with long purchase histories very slow.
symptom: The slowest io-shop requests took far longer to load
causal_chain 1: The slowest requests to io-shop took far longer than usual. Its slowest-request latency rose from the minute the incident began, and no more requests failed than before. (cites AL1; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2: Requests started going through the flag-on path when admin switched typical-purchase-feature on at {P1.1}. Before that, the service's flag evaluations were all off (Ga6f5). They were split during {Gc8c4.6} (Gc8c4) and all on from then until the alert (Gd44a). (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; Ga6f5, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc8c4, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gd44a, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2 ruled_out 2: Any other flag change: the flag provider's history showed no flag change by anyone but Argus other than this switch in the period read. (cites T15, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: With the flag on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item to build the shopper's spend summary. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix"; U1, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus")
causal_chain 4: Code-Fix read typical_spend_per_item's work as growing far faster than a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became slow. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: Before typical-purchase-feature was switched on, no check was seen that measured the latency of the code path it enabled for shoppers with long purchase histories.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The slowdown on the flag-on path would have been found before production traffic took that path.
contributing_factors 2: The flag was switched on for all traffic in one step: evaluations went from all off to all on almost immediately, and no gradual rollout was seen.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of requests would have taken the slow path at first, and the rise could have been caught and the flag turned off before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors 3: No test was seen that bounds how much work typical_spend_per_item does on a long purchase history.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: The function's growth with history length would have been caught in testing before any flag sent requests to it.
action_items 1: Before any feature flag that enables a new code path is switched on in production, require a latency check of that path against accounts with long purchase histories.
action_items 2: Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of traffic first, and widen them only while slowest-request latency stays at baseline.
action_items 3: Link the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person.
action_items 4: Make average_spend_per_item in spend_summary.py scale to long histories, and add a test that bounds its work. This is the flag-off path, which Code-Fix read as also growing far faster than history length.
went_wrong 1: The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
